Two Libyan soldiers died from injuries sustained in a weekend Ukrainian naval drone attack on Russian vessels moored at the Benghazi Naval Base, according to statements from eastern Libyan authorities. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky claimed responsibility for the operation, stating that Ukrainian forces deployed seven sea drones that struck a Russian navy corvette and a cargo ship on Sunday. Libyan authorities reported that the targeted corvette had docked at the base to refuel and rearm before the assault triggered regional condemnation. French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot defended the strikes as legitimate self-defense, while Italian officials raised concerns over Mediterranean stability.

Divers recovered the bodies of six occupants from the fuselage of a downed Cessna 210 in the Gulf of Mexico after an hourslong search operation. The aircraft carried four adults and two boys, aged 8 and 10, when it crashed two miles northeast of Horn Island. The air traffic control regional tower in Mobile, Alabama, reported losing contact with the flight at approximately 3:45 p.m. Preliminary Federal Aviation Administration data indicated the plane was descending at 10,000 feet per minute into the water. Both the Federal Aviation Administration and the National Transportation Safety Board are investigating the incident.

Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called a snap general election in Spain for November 29 after parliament rejected proposed decrees addressing rising rents and evictions following national protests over an 87-year-old woman evicted in Madrid. Conservative leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo promoted the deregulation model implemented in Madrid during campaign debates. Sanchez highlighted Socialist-led Catalonia measures such as rent caps and bans on short-term rentals to combat the affordability crisis. Think-tank FEDEA data indicates high demand with hundreds of enquiries per available home in Catalonia and Madrid.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport reinstated Senegal as the 2025 Africa Cup of Nations winner after upholding an appeal against their disqualification. The ruling sets aside the Confederation of African Football Appeal Board decision that previously awarded the title to Morocco as a 3-0 default win. The legal dispute stemmed from the January 18 final in Rabat, where Senegal players briefly walked off the pitch during second-half stoppage time after referee Jean-Jacques Ndala awarded Morocco a penalty. The original final match had ended in a 1-0 extra-time victory for Senegal against Morocco before the administrative penalties were applied.

Nidal Hasan filed a motion in a federal court in Topeka, Kansas, seeking a stay of his scheduled December 3 execution by firing squad. Imprisoned at Fort Leavenworth, Hasan stated in the filing that he intends to demonstrate his military court judgment and death sentence violated his federal constitutional and statutory rights due to unlawful command influence. U.S. District Judge Anthony Mattivi scheduled a hearing regarding the stay of execution for Wednesday morning. The American Civil Liberties Union and the ACLU of Kansas are acting as standby counsel for Hasan, who was convicted by a military jury in August 2013 of 13 counts of premeditated murder for the 2009 shooting at Fort Hood.

President Donald Trump stated in an Oval Office interview with the New York Post that he will meet with incoming Michigan Democratic Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed to discuss healthcare policy. El-Sayed recently posted a mockup of a golden TrumpCare card on social media, urging the president to embrace a single-payer healthcare system by attaching his name to it. Trump called the branding very smart and praised the Michigan Democrat's approach, noting that a middle ground could potentially be reached. El-Sayed is a Democrat elected to represent Michigan who will take office in January.

China launched the Shenzhou-24 spacecraft from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center using a Long March-2F rocket, carrying a three-member crew that includes Pakistan's first astronaut, Muhammad Zeeshan Ali. The spacecraft successfully docked with the Tiangong space station roughly three and a half hours after liftoff. Ali, a 40-year-old pilot serving as a payload specialist, became the first foreign national to board the Chinese space station. He is flying alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi on the orbital mission.

North Korea expelled the head of Switzerland's diplomatic office in Pyongyang, Sylvain Astier, declaring him persona non grata and ordering him to leave the country within 48 hours. The Foreign Ministry handed Astier a memorandum demanding the closure of the office in response to Switzerland's decision to impose sanctions on the Songdowon International Children's Camp. Switzerland added the camp to its sanctions list on November 4, alleging its involvement in the transfer and ideological conditioning of Ukrainian children. Kim Yo Jong publicly denounced the Swiss sanctions prior to the expulsion order.

A federal grand jury has been empaneled in Washington, D.C., to hear evidence regarding a long-running immigration fraud investigation into Representative Ilhan Omar and her family members. Prosecutors from the D.C. U.S. Attorney's Office and the Minnesota U.S. Attorney's Office are examining matters dating back to 1980, including whether Omar misrepresented her birth date on government paperwork to obtain U.S. citizenship through her father's naturalization in 2000. Federal law enforcement agents previously executed a search warrant at Omar's Washington home in October as part of the unsealed probe.

Yemen's Houthi movement claimed responsibility for attacks targeting Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and the King Abdullah Financial District in Riyadh. Eleven people were injured in the Houthi drone strike on a tower in Riyadh's financial district, including two Saudi nationals, two Indian nationals, three Nepalis, and four Egyptians. India's Ministry of External Affairs confirmed the injuries of its two nationals and strongly condemned the attack. The Saudi-led coalition stated that air defenses intercepted and destroyed four drones over the Ras Tanura refinery in the Eastern Province.

Relatives of the slain men subsequently set fire to homes belonging to members of the banned Awami League.

B: Factory workers in Dhaka also engaged in protests, setting fire to government vehicles and ransacking factories, resulting in the closure of twenty-eight factories and losses to the garment industry. ## OPINION | Exile Demands No State Aircraft From The People She Fled
A: This is Void Opinion. Through a progressive lens today. Exile demands no state aircraft from the people she fled.
A: Sheikh Hasina abandoned Bangladesh on August fifth, two thousand twenty-four, leaving behind a death toll of fourteen hundred people recorded by the United Nations after security forces suppressed a student-led mass uprising. An International Crimes Tribunal subsequently sentenced the deposed leader to the death penalty in absentia. The spokesperson formally requested that the current administration provide air transport aboard the national carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines, for her journey originating from Delhi. This juxtaposition between official criminal proceedings and an exiled leader demanding VIP state logistics exposes a fundamental fracture in transitional accountability.
A: We watch accountability tested when ousted rulers demand the apparatus of the very state they damaged to facilitate their reentry. The mechanics of this return request reveal an impunity that institutional justice exists to dismantle. State resources belong to the public rather than to individuals judicially condemned for mass casualty events. When an exiled leader demands a national carrier flight while facing a death sentence, the system must choose between enforcing its own verdicts and capitulating to historical privilege.
A: We recognize that territorial proximity and bilateral asylum arrangements complicate the logistics of enforcing international criminal sentences across borders. We insist that the state aircraft remains grounded for anyone fleeing criminal conviction. State power must serve the victims of violence rather than the architects of suppression. Returning to face accountability means submitting to handcuffs and tribunals, not booking VIP seats on national airlines. We refuse to accept that exile erases the debt owed to a society that buried fourteen hundred victims of state violence.

opinion_text:
Sheikh Hasina abandoned Bangladesh on August 5, 2024, leaving behind a death toll of 1,400 people recorded by the United Nations after security forces suppressed a student-led mass uprising. An International Crimes Tribunal subsequently sentenced the deposed leader to the death penalty in absentia. Her spokesperson, Syed Mozammel Ali, announced a planned return to Dhaka on December 16, coinciding with the anniversary of the end of the 1971 war with Pakistan. The spokesperson formally requested that the current administration provide air transport aboard the national carrier, Biman Bangladesh Airlines, for her journey originating from Delhi.

State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir stated that any return must occur through formal extradition involving handcuffs and strict surveillance. International Crimes Tribunal Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam characterized the demand for a state-provided aircraft as madness. This juxtaposition between official criminal proceedings and an exiled leader demanding VIP state logistics exposes a fundamental fracture in transitional accountability.

We watch accountability tested when ousted rulers demand the apparatus of the very state they damaged to facilitate their reentry. The mechanics of this return request reveal an impunity that institutional justice exists to dismantle. State resources belong to the public rather than to individuals judicially condemned for mass casualty events. When an exiled leader demands a national carrier flight while facing a death sentence, the system must choose between enforcing its own verdicts and capitulating to historical privilege.

We recognize that territorial proximity and bilateral asylum arrangements complicate the logistics of enforcing international criminal sentences across borders. India houses the former prime minister, while Dhaka demands extradition under guard. This diplomatic friction turns a legal mandate into a geopolitical chess match. Yet the presence of a judicial sentence and an extradition requirement leaves little room for negotiated pageantry.

Justice requires that power remain subordinate to the rule of law rather than the whims of fallen executives. We insist that the state aircraft remains grounded for anyone fleeing criminal conviction. State power must serve the victims of violence rather than the architects of suppression. Returning to face accountability means submitting to handcuffs and tribunals, not booking VIP seats on national airlines. We refuse to accept that exile erases the debt owed to a society that buried 1,400 victims of state violence.

Now, void opinion.

Through a progressive lens today.

Exile Demands No State Aircraft From The People She Fled.

Sheikh Hasina boarded a flight out of Bangladesh on August 5, 2024, escaping a student-led uprising and leaving behind 1,400 dead bodies counted by the United Nations. An International Crimes Tribunal tried her and handed down a death sentence in absentia. Now, her spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali announces she plans to fly back on December 16, exactly on the anniversary marking the end of the 1971 war.

She wants the Dhaka administration to send Biman Bangladesh Airlines to Delhi to fetch her. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir answers that she can only return through extradition in handcuffs and under strict surveillance. International Crimes Tribunal Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam calls the demand for a state plane madness.

We find ourselves confronting the audacity of fallen power. The apparatus of the state is not a personal taxi service for leaders who fled accountability. When a court condemns someone to death for orchestrating mass killings, the response to a demand for state air transport cannot be negotiation. It must be the cold implementation of an extradition warrant.

We know that borders and diplomatic sanctuaries complicate the mechanics of justice. India holds her. Bangladesh wants her in irons. But the ledger of a democratic transition balances on whether a judicial sentence applies universally or bends for former rulers.

We demand that the institutions built to protect the public do not flinch before the ghosts of authoritarianism. A state aircraft belongs to the people, not to the condemned. Let her return through the handcuffs and the courtrooms she avoided.

This was void opinion.
